content.text: Magnetism is a fundamental force of nature that has been known to humans for thousands of years. The ancient Greeks discovered that a naturally occurring mineral called lodestone (a form of iron oxide) could attract pieces of iron. The Chinese used magnetic compasses for navigation as early as the 11th century. Today, magnetism is essential to countless technologies, from electric motors and generators to computer hard drives and medical imaging machines.

In this lesson, we will explore the basic properties of magnets, magnetic fields, the difference between magnetic and non-magnetic materials, methods of making and destroying magnets, and the Earth's own magnetic field.

Magnetic field lines can be plotted using two methods:
Place a bar magnet on a sheet of paper.
Place a small plotting compass near the north pole of the magnet.
Mark the position of both ends of the compass needle (a dot at each end).
Move the compass so that its south end is at the position where the north end was.
Again mark the positions of both ends.
Repeat until you reach the south pole of the magnet (or the edge of the paper).
Connect the dots to form a smooth field line. Add an arrow showing the direction (north to south outside the magnet).
Repeat for different starting positions to build up the full field pattern.
Place a bar magnet under a sheet of paper or a transparent plastic sheet.
Sprinkle iron filings evenly over the sheet.
Gently tap the sheet so the filings can align with the magnetic field.
The filings form a pattern that shows the shape of the field lines.
The iron filings method is quick and shows the overall field pattern, but it does not show the direction of the field lines. The compass method shows direction but is more time-consuming.

A student has two iron bars, A and B. One is a magnet and the other is not. Without using any other equipment, how can the student determine which is the magnet?
Bring one end of bar A near the
If bar A is the magnet, it will attract the middle of bar B (because it induces magnetism in bar B).
Now bring one end of bar B near the
If bar B is the magnet, it will attract the middle of bar A.
The key test: bring the end of one bar to the

of the other. A magnet is strongest at its poles (ends) and weakest at its centre. If bar A is not a magnet, its end will be attracted to the middle of bar B (the magnet) because the end of bar A will have induced magnetism. But if bar A is a magnet, its end will still attract the middle of bar B (which is not a magnet).

The definitive approach: if one bar attracts the other at the centre as well as at the ends, the bar being attracted at its centre is NOT the magnet (a magnet has its weakest point at the centre). Alternatively, try to find repulsion — if you can find a combination of ends that repel, both bars are magnets. If no repulsion is found, and one bar shows no effect when its middle is brought near the end of the other, that bar is the non-magnet.
The simplest method: hold bar A by its middle and touch the end of bar A to the middle of bar B. If there is attraction, swap and try the reverse. The one that shows
no attraction when its middle is brought to the end of the other
is the magnet, because the middle of a magnet is its weakest point.

Describe how to use the compass method to plot the magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
Place the bar magnet on a large sheet of white paper and draw around it.
Place a small plotting compass near the north pole of the magnet.
Use a pencil to mark a dot at each end of the compass needle.
Move the compass so that the tail (south-seeking end) of the needle is at the position where the tip (north-seeking end) was.
Mark the new positions of the needle tips.
Repeat step 4 and 5, following the field line until you reach the south pole of the magnet or the edge of the paper.
Join the dots with a smooth curved line.
Add an arrowhead pointing from north to south (the direction the north end of the compass pointed).
Repeat the process starting from different positions around the north pole to plot several field lines.

While permanent magnets retain their magnetism for a long time, they can be demagnetised by heating, hammering, or exposure to alternating magnetic fields. Their strength also decreases very slowly over time.
"The magnetic field only exists between the poles."
The magnetic field extends all around the magnet, not just between the poles. It is strongest at the poles, but field lines exist on all sides.

Explain why repulsion is the only sure test for magnetism.

A magnet can attract both another magnet and an unmagnetised piece of magnetic material (through induced magnetism). Therefore, attraction alone does not prove both objects are magnets — one could be unmagnetised iron. However, repulsion can only occur between two magnets with like poles facing each other. An unmagnetised object cannot be repelled by a magnet. So
is the definitive proof that both objects are magnets.

Explain how stroking magnetises an iron bar using domain theory.

In an unmagnetised iron bar, the magnetic domains point in random directions. When a permanent magnet is repeatedly stroked along the bar in one direction, the magnetic field of the stroking magnet causes the domains to rotate and align in the same direction as the applied field. After many strokes, most domains are aligned, and the bar has a net magnetic field — it is magnetised.
Describe one method of magnetisation and one of demagnetisation for steel.
Place the steel bar inside a solenoid and pass a large direct current (DC) through the coil. The strong, uniform magnetic field inside the solenoid aligns the domains in the steel.

Place the steel bar inside a solenoid carrying alternating current (AC). The constantly reversing field randomises the domains. Slowly withdraw the bar from the solenoid while the AC is still flowing.
